pages.title: What is globalisation: McLuhan, Friedman, Giddens
pages.summary: Globalisation is explained through the global village (McLuhan), borderless world (Ohmae), flat world (Friedman) and time-space compression (Giddens). Friedman defines it as interaction becoming farther, faster, deeper and cheaper, and the notes say it is neither a myth nor a buzzword.

pages.title: Responses to globalisation: Marxists, Islamic societies, Parekh
pages.summary: Responses are mixed in both developed and developing countries. Marxists oppose the present model as global expansion of capitalism, Islamic societies see an attempt to spread western values, and Bhikhu Parekh proposes a cosmopolitan globalisation through dialogue, with the Indian model based on Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

pages.title: Jagdish Bhagwati's defence of globalisation
pages.summary: Bhagwati, in In Defence of Globalisation, argues that globalisation has brought unprecedented growth to poor countries and growth is trickling down, citing falling poverty, higher life expectancy, lower child mortality and rising literacy. He admits it is no solution by itself but calls it the most powerful social good if properly governed.

pages.title: Wallerstein, Chomsky, and Heine-Thakur's critique
pages.summary: Wallerstein sees nothing new, only capitalist exploitation since the 17th century now dying, with the choice being socialism or barbarianism. Chomsky's Profit over People says security policy subsidises arms dealers and capitalist states fight wars to open markets, and Heine and Thakur's The Dark Side of Globalisation is introduced.

pages.title: Dark side of globalisation: aid versus illegal flows
pages.summary: Heine and Thakur contrast development aid of 50 to 80 billion dollars a year from north to south with 500 to 800 billion dollars of goods moving illegally from south to north. They add that wage share has fallen, workers' bargaining power has declined, Guinea Bissau became a narco state, and globalisation has given rise to uncivil society.

pages.title: Joseph Stiglitz on inequality and democratic deficit
pages.summary: Stiglitz, in Democracy and its Discontent and Making Globalisation Work, highlights inter- and intra-state inequality, financial crises and the democratic deficit in global governance. He argues globalisation benefited the top 1 percent plutocrats in developed countries, hurt their middle and working classes, benefited rich people in developing countries and middle classes in emerging economies, and hurt the poor.

pages.title: Roy, Mehta, and Sen on globalisation
pages.summary: Arundhati Roy calls neo-liberal capitalism a mutant variety of colonialism, and Pratap Bhanu Mehta says anti-globalisation sentiment now comes from northern middle and working classes, fuelling right-wing xenophobia and plutocracy. Amartya Sen says countries that joined globalisation are better off but benefits are uneven, so capacity building of people is needed.

pages.title: Lagarde and Summers on inequality and nationalism
pages.summary: IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde acknowledged that rising inequality has become the Achilles heel of market-driven globalisation, with little optimism. Larry Summers of Harvard recommends a return to responsible nationalism and sensible international cooperation.

flashcards.front: How does Thomas Friedman define globalisation in The Lexus and the Olive Tree?
flashcards.back: As the process by which nation states, corporations, civil societies and individuals interact at an unprecedented level, making interaction farther, faster, deeper and cheaper. The notes pair this with McLuhan's global village, Ohmae's borderless world and Giddens's time-space compression.

flashcards.front: What alternative to the western model of globalisation do the notes offer, and who recommends a cosmopolitan form?
flashcards.back: Bhikhu Parekh recommends a cosmopolitan globalisation based on dialogue between civilisations. The notes cite the Indian model based on Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and Sarve Bhavantu Sukhinah, and the Islamic concept of brotherhood.

flashcards.front: What are Jagdish Bhagwati's main arguments in defence of globalisation?
flashcards.back: It has brought unprecedented growth to poor countries, growth is trickling down and inequality is diminishing. He cites poverty on a dollar a day halved in 20 years, almost doubled life expectancy, falling child mortality and literacy rising from 59 percent to 80 percent by 2000, but says it must be properly governed.

flashcards.front: What is Immanuel Wallerstein's view of present-day globalisation?
flashcards.back: Nothing is new: it continues capitalist exploitation going on since the 17th century, and poverty in Africa or wars in the Balkans stem from the capitalist search for markets. He says it is dying, and people must choose between socialism and barbarianism.

flashcards.front: Who benefits and who loses from globalisation according to Joseph Stiglitz?
flashcards.back: It benefited the 1 percent plutocrats in developed countries but hurt their middle and working classes. It benefited rich people in developing countries and middle classes in emerging economies, and adversely impacted the poor.

flashcards.front: What do Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Amartya Sen each say about globalisation?
flashcards.back: Mehta says anti-globalisation sentiment now comes from middle and working classes in the North, bringing right-wing xenophobia and plutocracy. Sen says countries that joined globalisation are better placed than those that opted out, but benefits are uneven, so capacity building of people is needed.

answers.question: Critically examine the debate between supporters and critics of globalisation, with reference to Bhagwati, Wallerstein, Stiglitz, and Heine and Thakur.
answers.intro: Globalisation, captured by ideas such as the global village and time-space compression, is neither a myth nor a buzzword. Responses are mixed in both developed and developing societies, with some groups benefiting and others seeing it as anti-growth.
body: Jagdish Bhagwati, in In Defence of Globalisation, argues it has brought unprecedented growth to poor countries, with poverty halved, life expectancy almost doubled, child mortality down and literacy up from 59 to 80 percent. He adds that if properly governed it is the most powerful social good.

Immanuel Wallerstein sees only the old capitalist exploitation of the 17th century, now dying, leaving the choice between socialism and barbarianism. Marxists in general oppose the present model as capitalism on a global scale.

Heine and Thakur in The Dark Side of Globalisation contrast aid of 50 to 80 billion dollars with 500 to 800 billion dollars of illegal flows from south to north, and note falling wage share and the rise of narco states and uncivil society.
Joseph Stiglitz stresses inequality and the democratic deficit in global governance, saying it benefited 1 percent plutocrats and hurt middle and working classes.
Amartya Sen finds participants better off but unevenly, calling for capacity building.
answers.conclusion: Both sides use evidence: Bhagwati shows gains in growth and welfare, while critics show rising inequality and illegal flows. Even Sen and Lagarde accept uneven benefits, so the task is to govern globalisation fairly, with capacity building and international cooperation.
